prompt: Which of the following best defines a business cycle?

options.label: A
options.text: A fixed, calendar-based schedule in which the economy expands for exactly two years and contracts for exactly one year.

options.label: B
options.text: Recurring fluctuations in aggregate output and employment caused by changes in aggregate supply and/or aggregate demand.

options.label: C
options.text: The long-run upward trend of potential output that results from the accumulation of productive capacity over decades.

options.label: D
options.text: The difference between the peak level of real GDP and the trough level of real GDP within a single contraction.

options.label: E
options.text: A government-mandated sequence of monetary and fiscal actions designed to stabilize prices across time.

explanation: defines business cycles as fluctuations in aggregate output and employment that arise from changes in aggregate supply and/or aggregate demand. They are not fixed in length or caused solely by policy; they represent the short-run ups and downs of the economy around its long-run growth trend.

prompt: According to the CED, what are the TWO phases of a business cycle?

options.label: A
options.text: Peak and trough.

options.label: B
options.text: Inflation and deflation.

options.label: C
options.text: Recession and expansion.

options.label: D
options.text: Contraction and stagnation.

options.label: E
options.text: Output gap and potential output.

explanation: identifies recession and expansion as the two phases of a business cycle; recession is the contractionary phase (falling output and employment); expansion is the growth phase (rising output and employment); peak and trough are turning points, not phases.

prompt: What are the TWO turning points of a business cycle?

options.label: A
options.text: Recession and expansion.

options.label: B
options.text: Aggregate supply and aggregate demand.

options.label: C
options.text: Potential output and actual output.

options.label: D
options.text: Peak and trough.

options.label: E
options.text: Output gap and full-employment output.

explanation: identifies peak and trough as the turning points of a business cycle; the peak is the high point where an expansion ends and recession begins; the trough is the low point where a recession ends and expansion begins.

prompt: A peak in the business cycle is best described as

options.label: A
options.text: the lowest point of a recession, after which real GDP begins to recover.

options.label: B
options.text: the point at which actual output equals potential output and the output gap is zero.

options.label: C
options.text: the highest point of an expansion, after which real GDP begins to fall and the economy enters the recessionary phase.

options.label: D
options.text: the point at which the output gap is most negative during a contraction.

options.label: E
options.text: the long-run level of output consistent with full employment of all resources.

explanation: A peak is the turning point at which an expansion reaches its highest level of real GDP and transitions into the recessionary phase. After the peak, output and employment both fall; it is not a point of zero output gap by definition - peaks may occur above, at, or below potential output.

prompt: A trough in the business cycle is best described as

options.label: A
options.text: the highest point of an expansion, marking the transition to recession.

options.label: B
options.text: the level of real GDP at which the economy produces at its full-employment capacity.

options.label: C
options.text: the point at which the output gap is positive and actual output exceeds potential.

options.label: D
options.text: the lowest point of a recession, after which real GDP begins to rise and the economy enters the expansionary phase.

options.label: E
options.text: the phase during which aggregate output and employment are both falling.

explanation: A trough is the turning point at which a recession reaches its lowest level of real GDP and transitions into the expansionary phase. After the trough, output and employment begin to rise; the trough is the mirror image of the peak: peaks mark the start of contractions, troughs mark the end of contractions.

prompt: The output gap is defined as

options.label: A
options.text: the difference between the peak level and trough level of actual output in a business cycle.

options.label: B
options.text: the difference between nominal GDP and real GDP in a given year.

options.label: C
options.text: the difference between actual output and potential output.

options.label: D
options.text: the difference between aggregate demand and aggregate supply at a given price level.

options.label: E
options.text: the difference between full-employment output and the natural rate of unemployment.

explanation: Output gap = Actual output - Potential output; when positive, actual exceeds potential (inflationary gap); when negative, actual falls short of potential (recessionary gap); when zero, the economy is at potential output.

prompt: Potential output is also known as

options.label: A
options.text: peak output, because it represents the highest real GDP the economy ever achieves.

options.label: B
options.text: full-employment output — the level of GDP produced when unemployment equals the natural rate.

options.label: C
options.text: trough output, because it represents the minimum sustainable level of production.

options.label: D
options.text: zero-gap output, meaning actual output is always exactly equal to this benchmark.

options.label: E
options.text: cyclical output, because it fluctuates with each phase of the business cycle.

explanation: The CED explicitly states that potential output is "also called full-employment output." It is the level of GDP consistent with unemployment equaling the natural rate (frictional + structural, no cyclical unemployment). It is not a ceiling - actual output can temporarily exceed it.

prompt: When actual output is below potential output, the output gap is

options.label: A
options.text: positive, indicating the economy is in an inflationary gap.

options.label: B
options.text: zero, because the output gap is only defined when actual equals potential.

options.label: C
options.text: negative, indicating a recessionary gap — the economy is underproducing relative to its full-employment capacity.

options.label: D
options.text: undefined, because output gaps only exist during peaks and troughs.

options.label: E
options.text: positive, because potential output is always lower than actual output during recessions.

explanation: Output gap = Actual - Potential; when actual < potential, the result is negative - a recessionary (negative) gap; unemployment exceeds the natural rate and productive capacity is underutilized; the economy is operating inside its full-employment frontier.

prompt: When actual output is above potential output, the output gap is

options.label: A
options.text: negative, indicating a recessionary gap with high unemployment.

options.label: B
options.text: zero, because actual output cannot exceed potential output.

options.label: C
options.text: positive, indicating an inflationary gap — the economy is temporarily operating beyond its full-employment capacity with unemployment below the natural rate.

options.label: D
options.text: negative, because exceeding potential always contracts the economy.

options.label: E
options.text: undefined, because potential output is a theoretical maximum that can never be surpassed.

explanation: Output gap = Actual - Potential; when actual > potential, the result is positive - an inflationary (positive) gap. Unemployment has fallen below the natural rate and the economy is temporarily overextending its resources; this is unsustainable and typically generates upward wage and price pressure.

prompt: According to MEA-2.A.5, potential output is the level of GDP at which

options.label: A
options.text: actual output reaches its highest point during a business cycle expansion.

options.label: B
options.text: the output gap is at its most negative value.

options.label: C
options.text: aggregate supply and aggregate demand intersect at a price level of 100.

options.label: D
options.text: unemployment equals the natural rate of unemployment.

options.label: E
options.text: the economy has zero inflation and zero unemployment simultaneously.

explanation: Potential output is precisely defined as the GDP level where unemployment = the natural rate; at this point, only frictional and structural unemployment exist; cyclical unemployment is zero; the output gap is zero; this is the economy's sustainable full-employment benchmark.

prompt: During a recession, both aggregate output and employment

options.label: A
options.text: rise, reflecting increased productive capacity.

options.label: B
options.text: fall — MEA-2.A.1 defines business cycle fluctuations as involving declines in both aggregate output AND employment during the contractionary phase.

options.label: C

options.label: D
options.text: rise above potential output, creating an inflationary gap.

options.label: E
options.text: become equal to potential output as the economy self-corrects.

explanation: MEA-2.A.2: Business cycles are defined as fluctuations in BOTH aggregate output AND employment; during a recession (the contractionary phase), real GDP falls and employment declines simultaneously, because firms produce less and therefore need fewer workers.

prompt: During an expansion, both aggregate output and employment

options.label: A
options.text: fall, as the economy approaches its trough.

options.label: B
options.text: remain constant at the natural rate of unemployment.

options.label: C
options.text: rise — during the expansionary phase, real GDP increases and firms hire more workers, raising employment alongside rising output.

options.label: D
options.text: move in opposite directions: output rises while employment falls.

options.label: E
options.text: fall below potential output, widening the recessionary gap.

explanation: MEA-2.A.2: During an expansion (the growth phase), real GDP rises and firms hire more workers to meet increased demand - employment rises alongside output; both dimensions of MEA-2.A.1 move together in the same direction: up during expansion, down during recession.

prompt: Which of the following correctly sequences a complete business cycle beginning at the trough?

options.label: A
options.text: Trough → Peak → Expansion → Recession → Trough

options.label: E
options.text: Expansion → Recession → Trough → Peak → Expansion

explanation: MEA-2.A.3: Starting from the trough (lowest point), the economy enters the expansionary phase (rising output and employment), reaches the peak (highest turning point), then enters the recessionary phase (falling output and employment), and returns to the next trough. Trough → Expansion → Peak → Recession → Trough completes one full cycle.

prompt: According to MEA-2.A.1, business cycles are caused by changes in

options.label: A

options.label: B

options.label: C

explanation: explicitly states that business cycles result from "changes in aggregate supply and/or aggregate demand." Any shock - whether a change in consumer confidence (AD), a supply disruption (AS), fiscal policy (AD), or a technology improvement (AS) - generates business cycle fluctuations through these two channels.

prompt: When the output gap equals zero, which of the following must be true?

options.label: A
options.text: The economy is at a business cycle peak.

options.label: B
options.text: Unemployment is zero and all labor is fully employed.

options.label: C
options.text: The economy is in the recessionary phase with falling real GDP.

options.label: D
options.text: Actual output equals potential output and unemployment equals the natural rate of unemployment.

options.label: E

explanation: MEA-2.A.5: Output gap = 0 means Actual = Potential; by MEA-2.A.5, potential output is defined as GDP at the natural rate of unemployment. Therefore, zero output gap implies unemployment = natural rate and cyclical unemployment = 0; the economy is at its full-employment benchmark, not necessarily at a cyclical peak.

prompt: At the business cycle trough, which of the following is most likely true?

options.label: A
options.text: Actual output equals potential output and the output gap is zero.

options.label: B
options.text: The economy is in the expansionary phase with rising employment.

options.label: C
options.text: Actual output is at its lowest relative to potential — the recessionary gap is at its deepest — and unemployment is at its cyclical high.

options.label: D
options.text: The output gap is positive and the economy is overheating.

options.label: E
options.text: Potential output falls to meet actual output, closing the recessionary gap.

explanation: MEA-2.A.4: The trough is the lowest point of a recession. Actual output is at its cyclical minimum, furthest below potential - the recessionary gap is most negative; employment is at its cyclical low and unemployment is at its cyclical peak; after the trough, the expansion begins and the gap begins to close.

prompt: At the business cycle peak, which of the following is most likely true?

options.label: A
options.text: Actual output is at its cyclical minimum and the output gap is most negative.

options.label: B
options.text: The economy has just entered the recessionary phase with rapidly falling employment.

options.label: C
options.text: Real GDP is at its cyclical high and unemployment is at or near its cyclical low — the economy transitions from expansion to recession.

options.label: D
options.text: The output gap is negative and potential output exceeds actual output.

options.label: E
options.text: The economy has reached zero unemployment and the recessionary gap is eliminated.

explanation: At the peak, actual real GDP is at its cyclical maximum - the expansion has reached its high point. Employment is near its cyclical peak and unemployment near its cyclical low; after the peak, the economy enters the recessionary phase: output and employment begin to fall.

prompt: A recessionary gap exists when

options.label: A
options.text: actual output exceeds potential output and unemployment is below the natural rate.

options.label: B
options.text: actual output equals potential output and the economy is at full employment.

options.label: C
options.text: potential output falls to zero during a severe contraction.

options.label: D
options.text: actual output is below potential output — the output gap is negative, indicating the economy is underperforming relative to its full-employment capacity with unemployment above the natural rate.

options.label: E
options.text: the economy is between trough and peak during a strong expansion.

explanation: MEA-2.A.5: A recessionary gap (negative output gap) exists when actual output < potential output. This means unemployment > natural rate (cyclical unemployment is positive); the economy has unused productive capacity - workers and capital are idle; recessionary gaps are associated with the contractionary phase and its aftermath.

prompt: An inflationary gap exists when

options.label: A
options.text: the price level rises above the GDP deflator in the base year.

options.label: B
options.text: actual output is below potential output and unemployment exceeds the natural rate.

options.label: C
options.text: actual output exceeds potential output — the economy is temporarily producing beyond its sustainable full-employment capacity, with unemployment below the natural rate.

options.label: D
options.text: the economy has passed its trough and is in early-stage expansion.

options.label: E
options.text: government spending on output increases aggregate demand past the natural rate.

explanation: MEA-2.A.5: An inflationary gap (positive output gap) exists when actual > potential. Unemployment has fallen below the natural rate; the economy is overextending its resources; this is unsustainable - upward wage and price pressure typically brings the economy back toward potential over time.

prompt: Which of the following correctly describes the relationship between potential output and the natural rate of unemployment?

options.label: A
options.text: Potential output is the GDP level consistent with zero unemployment.

options.label: B
options.text: The natural rate and potential output are unrelated — one measures labor markets, the other measures output.

options.label: C
options.text: Potential output is the GDP level produced when unemployment equals the natural rate — the two are directly linked by definition in MEA-2.A.5.

options.label: D
options.text: The natural rate of unemployment equals the output gap divided by potential output.

options.label: E
options.text: Potential output rises whenever the natural rate of unemployment rises.

explanation: The CED directly defines potential output as "the level of GDP where unemployment is equal to the natural rate of unemployment." The two are inseparable: the natural rate defines the unemployment benchmark for full employment, and potential output is the corresponding GDP produced at that benchmark.

prompt: Which of the following best describes the long-run trend of potential output on a business cycle graph?

options.label: A
options.text: Potential output is a flat horizontal line, because the economy's productive capacity never changes.

options.label: B
options.text: Potential output oscillates above and below actual output throughout the business cycle.

options.label: C

options.label: E
options.text: Potential output equals actual output at every point, so both lines are identical on the graph.

explanation: (graph): The CED business cycle graph shows potential output as an upward-trending line reflecting long-run growth in the economy's productive capacity (driven by capital, labor, and technology improvements). Actual GDP is a wave-like curve that oscillates above and below this rising potential output trend.

prompt: During which phase of the business cycle is cyclical unemployment at its highest level?

options.label: A
options.text: During the expansionary phase, when firms are aggressively hiring.

options.label: B
options.text: At the business cycle peak, when employment is at its cyclical high.

options.label: C
options.text: At or near the trough — the economy has completed its contraction and cyclical unemployment peaks at the end of the recessionary phase before recovery begins.

options.label: D
options.text: During periods when the output gap is positive and actual output exceeds potential.

options.label: E
options.text: When potential output grows faster than actual output during a sustained expansion.

explanation: -A.5: Cyclical unemployment is highest when actual output is furthest below potential - at or near the trough. Throughout the recessionary phase, employment falls and cyclical unemployment builds; it reaches its peak at the trough (the most negative point of the output gap) before the expansion begins reducing it.

prompt: A decrease in aggregate demand would most likely cause which of the following business cycle events?

options.label: A
options.text: A shift of potential output to a higher level, raising full-employment GDP.

options.label: B
options.text: A positive output gap as actual output rises above potential.

options.label: C
options.text: The economy moving from peak to trough — falling aggregate demand reduces actual output and employment, initiating the recessionary phase of the business cycle.

options.label: D
options.text: An increase in potential output, which widens the inflationary gap.

options.label: E
options.text: The economy remaining at potential output because AD shifts do not affect real variables.

explanation: MEA-2.A.2: A decrease in AD is one of the primary drivers of business cycle contractions. Lower AD means firms face reduced demand for their output, so they cut production (output falls) and reduce hiring (employment falls); this pushes the economy from its peak into the recessionary phase, with actual output moving below potential and a recessionary gap developing.

prompt: A significant increase in aggregate supply would most likely cause which of the following?

options.label: A

options.label: B

options.label: E
options.text: The recessionary gap to widen as potential output rises faster than actual output.

explanation: MEA-2.A.2: Increases in AS (e.g., a positive technology shock) produce more real GDP and employment - the hallmarks of expansion. specifies that business cycles arise from changes in AS and/or AD; an AS increase is a supply-side driver of expansion, raising both the real output produced and the employment used to produce it.

prompt: On a standard business cycle graph, the area where actual real GDP is BELOW the potential output line represents

prompt: On a standard business cycle graph, the area where actual real GDP is ABOVE the potential output line represents

options.label: A

This typically occurs during the later stages of a strong expansion when the economy has temporarily overshot its full-employment capacity; unemployment < natural rate during this period.

prompt: Potential output does NOT equal zero unemployment. Which of the following correctly explains why?

options.label: A
options.text: Potential output requires zero unemployment by definition — the two are equivalent.

options.label: B
options.text: At potential output, only cyclical unemployment exists; all structural unemployment has been eliminated.

options.label: C
options.text: Potential output corresponds to the natural rate of unemployment, which includes frictional and structural unemployment — workers who are temporarily between jobs or displaced by structural change. Cyclical unemployment is zero, but the natural rate is positive.

options.label: D
options.text: Potential output requires unemployment above the natural rate to sustain long-run growth.

options.label: E
options.text: Zero unemployment would reduce potential output because fewer workers would seek employment.

explanation: At potential output, unemployment = natural rate, which includes frictional (people between jobs) and structural (skill-mismatch) unemployment. These forms persist even in a healthy economy; only cyclical unemployment (from insufficient AD) is zero at potential; the natural rate is typically around 4-6%, not zero.

prompt: Which of the following is an accurate statement comparing the peak and trough of a business cycle?

options.label: A
options.text: Both the peak and trough are phases of the business cycle, not turning points.

options.label: B
options.text: The peak represents the lowest level of actual output; the trough represents the highest.

options.label: C
options.text: The peak and trough are both points at which actual output equals potential output.

explanation: Peak and trough are both turning points that bookend the recessionary phase. The peak is the high point (expansion ends, recession begins); the trough is the low point (recession ends, expansion begins); together they define one complete recessionary episode; the expansionary phase similarly runs from trough to peak.

prompt: Business cycles are described as fluctuations in aggregate output AND employment. This means that

options.label: B
options.text: only employment fluctuates; output is determined solely by potential output.

options.label: E
options.text: employment leads output by exactly one business cycle phase in all economies.

explanation: The joint definition of business cycles - fluctuations in BOTH output AND employment - reflects the direct link between production and labor demand. Firms produce less by employing fewer workers (recession) and produce more by employing more workers (expansion); both dimensions move together as a consequence of shifts in aggregate supply and/or demand.

prompt: Which of the following is the best statement of the MEA-2 Enduring Understanding regarding business cycles and long-run growth?

options.label: A

options.label: B

options.label: E

Short-run business cycles represent temporary deviations of actual output above and below a rising long-run potential output trend. The two phenomena coexist simultaneously.

prompt:
